INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
Amicus curiae Connecticut Against Gun Violence
(“CAGV”) is a nonprofit organization that was
founded in 1993 in Fairfield County, Connecticut, after a five-year-old child was shot and killed in Bridgeport. After its founding, CAGV led the campaign that
produced the State’s first assault weapons law. For
more than thirty years, CAGV has worked to reduce
gun violence in Connecticut through public education,
grassroots organizing, and legislative advocacy.
CAGV’s work took on new urgency on December
14, 2012, when a gunman, armed with an assault
weapon, murdered twenty first graders and six teachers and administrators at Sandy Hook Elementary
School in Newtown. In the weeks that followed,
CAGV’s membership grew from roughly 35,000 to
nearly 150,000, many of them parents. CAGV mobilized those members, togeth er with local clergy and
civic organizations, to demand that the Connecticut
General Assembly take action. CAGV’s then-executive director took an active role in drafting proposed
legislation concerning assault weapons, and CAGV
supported the work of bipartisan legislators and law
enforcement until that legislation, Public Act 13-3
(“the 2013 Act”), was signed into law.
CAGV submits this brief to provide the Court with
an account, from the organization that led the effort
resulting in Connecticut’s assault weapons law, of

1 Amicus curiae states that this brief was not authored in whole

2


why and how the people of Connecticut and their
elected representatives worked with such urgency and
diligence to pass that critical law. That history shows
that Connecticut’s current assault weapons law,
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53-202a et seq. (“the Law”), is a bipartisan and constitutional response to as clear an example of an “unprecedented societal concern” as this
Court is ever likely to see, N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol
Ass’n v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1, 27 (2022), and that the Law
is consistent with the Second Amendment.

3


INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
At 9:35 A.M. on December 14, 2012, a twentyyear-old gunman shot his way into Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut. He carried
a Bushmaster AR-15-style assault weapon, modeled
on the military’s M-16 design, with detachable magazines capable of holding thirty rounds, along with
more than 300 rounds of ammunition. In less than
five minutes, he fired 154 of those rounds and murdered twenty first graders and six educators. This unprecedented tragedy impacted not only the families—
irrevocably shattered by it s violence—but also thousands of parents and concerned citizens throughout
the state of Connecticut.
Petitioners ask this Court to hold that the Second
Amendment forbade Connecticut from doing what its
citizens demanded: prohibiting weapons with unusually dangerous features from being sold in the State
so an event like Sandy Hook can never happen again.
That proposition is disturbing and wrong. Confronted
with a danger whose full magnitude Sandy Hook laid
bare, the Connecticut legislature made a deliberate
judgment that specific features make a firearm unusually dangerous. Drawing lines on that basis is precisely what this Nation’s tradition of firearms regulation has always permitted.  CAGV writes to tell the
Court how that law came to be.
For two decades before Sandy Hook, CAGV had
warned that the State’s 1993 assault weapons law left
gaps that permitted the sale of firearms nearly identical to the ones it prohibited. After December 14,
2012, the people of Connecticut and their legislators

4


came to share that concer n. Within days, residents
were organizing in living rooms and church halls;
within weeks, thousands were traveling to Hartford to
testify and to march. Legislators of both parties negotiated through the winter. A bipartisan task force
held hearings in Hartford and in Newtown itself; police chiefs from across the State testified in support;
and the bill that emerged was debated, amended, and
ultimately passed by wide bipartisan margins in both
chambers. In short, the 2013 Act was the product of
the ordinary democratic process working exactly as it
should.
In 2013, the State legislated by feature and category, and the Law retains that structure today. As
currently codified, for instance, the Law prohibits the
most dangerous rifles by name and other semiautomatic, centerfire rifles based on their features, such as
those that can accept a detachable magazine and have
at least one of the follow ing enumerated military-derived features: a folding or telescoping stock; a pistol
grip, thumbhole stock, or other grip that allows a finger other than the trigger finger to sit below the action; a forward pistol grip; a flash suppressor; or a grenade or flare launcher. Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 53-
202a(1)(B), (E)(i), 53-202c. S trip those features from
the non-listed rifles, and those rifles remain lawful, as
do the handguns, shotguns, and other firearms available to Connecticut’s law-abiding residents. The Law
thus “preserv[es] numerous legal alternatives for selfdefense and other lawful purposes.” Nat’l Ass’n for
Gun Rights v. Lamont, 153 F.4th 213, 222 (2d Cir.
2025) (decided with Grant v. Rovella , No. 23-1344),
cert. granted sub nom. Grant v. Higgins , No. 25-566
(U.S. June 30, 2026).

5


The Law is also consistent with this Court’s precedent. The Second Amendment right “is not unlimited,” District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 626
(2008). This Court has recognized a historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of “dangerous or unusual weapons,” United States v. Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680,
697 (2024) (quoting 4 William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England 149 (1769)), a principle
which has been held to “encompass[] those arms that
legislators determined were unusually dangerous because of their characteristics,” Lamont, 153 F.4th at
233 (emphasis omitted). And this Court has held that,
where a law regulating guns was passed to address an
“unprecedented societal concern”—as the Law was, in
responding to the horror of Sandy Hook—courts must
take “a more nuanced approach” to the historical inquiry. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 27. The Law readily satisfies that approach.
CAGV respectfully asks this Court to leave Connecticut’s judgment undisturbed and to affirm.
ARGUMENT
The Law restricts the sale and possession of certain firearms, so the Court will first ask whether “the
Second Amendment’s plain text covers” the conduct
the Law regulates. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 17. If it does
not, the inquiry ends. Lamont, 153 F.4th at 231. If it
does, the burden shifts to th e State to show that the
Law “is consistent with the principles that underpin
our regulatory tradition.” Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 692;
see Bruen, 597 U.S. at 24. That showing does not require “a historical twin,” only “a well-established and
representative historical analogue.” Bruen, 597 U.S.
at 30. And where a law responds to “unprecedented

6


societal concerns or dramatic technological changes,”
the Court takes “a more nuanced approach,” id. at 27,
asking whether the modern law is “relevantly similar”
to the laws our tradition permits, Rahimi, 602 U.S. at
692 (quoting Bruen, 597 U.S. at 29). That inquiry
turns on “how and why” the modern and historical
laws burden the right of armed self-defense, and on
whether those burdens are comparable and comparably justified. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 29.
CAGV leaves the plain-text question and the full
historical record to the parties and instead writes to
address three issues. First, the murder of twenty first
graders and six educators at Sandy Hook is exactly
the kind of “unprecedented societal concern” that calls
for a “more nuanced approach” to the history and tradition analysis. See infra Part I. Second, the Law
grew directly out of that unprecedented societal concern. See infra Part II. Third, the Law fits comfortably within a “nuanced” view of the history and tradition of firearms regulation that this Court must consult. See infra Part III.
I. Sandy Hook Is The Paradigmatic Example
Of An “Unprecedented Societal Concern”
To determine whether a case implicates an “unprecedented societal concern,” courts consider
whether the problem a modern law addresses is one
that “preoccupied the Founders in 1791 or the Reconstruction generation in 1868.” Bruen, 597 U.S. at 27;
see Rupp v. Bonta, 723 F. Supp. 3d 837, 879 (C.D. Cal.
2024), appeal held in abeyance, No. 24-2583 (9th Cir.).
The problem addressed by the Law—the availability
of weapons like the one us ed by the lone gunman at
Sandy Hook to murder twen ty first graders and six

7


educators inside their school in under five minutes—
is one that neither the Founding generation nor the
Reconstruction generation ever contemplated.2
Mass shootings on the sca le of Sandy Hook are a
distinctly modern phenomenon. 3 There was “no
known occurrence of a mass shooting resulting in double-digit fatalities” in the first 173 years after the Nation’s founding, and the fi rst shooting in which a single gunman killed ten or more people did not occur until 1949. Lamont, 153 F.4th at 239 (citation omitted).
Before December 14, 2012, Americans had experienced a number of mass shootings, including several

the dead were first graders. Six were the educators
who tried to protect them, including the school’s principal and psychologist, who ran toward the

The public response to the tragedy confirmed that
Sandy Hook presented a so cietal concern unlike any
Connecticut—or the country—had confronted before.
Before the legislature took up the issue, Connecticut
residents immediately began organizing in their own
communities—largely thanks to CAGV’s coordination. From the morning after the shooting, CAGV’s
then-executive director, Ron Pinciaro, fielded calls

II. Connecticut’s Law Reflects A Bipartisan Response To An Unprecedented Societal Concern
CAGV took an active role in helping the General
Assembly with proposed legislation. Pinciaro, supra,
at 491–92, 494. Headed by Mr. Pinciaro, CAGV had
twenty-five days, over the holidays, to submit finished
proposals to the Judiciary Committee for the start of
the 2013 session. Id. at 491–92. With the help of volunteer students from Yale Law School, Mr. Pinciaro
immersed himself in this Court’s Second Amendment
precedent and in the Nation’s early history of firearms
regulation. He also studied closely the federal assault
weapons ban that Congress had enacted in 1994 and
in particular its structure: a features test paired with
a list of specific prohibited weapons.14

Connecticut had already learned why that combination—a features test, not a list alone—was essential. In 1993, the General Assembly enacted the
State’s first assault weapons statute. See An Act Concerning Assault Weapons, 1993 Conn. Pub. Acts No.
93-306. Michael Lawlor, then a member of the Judiciary Committee and the bill’s House floor manager,
recalls that Connecticut was confronting a serious
gun-violence problem and encountering AR-15-style
rifles for the first time.15 With the support of
Gover-nor Lowell Weicker, a divided House debated
the bill late into the night, and most of that debate
centered on a single question: What is an “assault
weapon”? The 1993 Act’s answer was a list: aside from
selective-fire firearms, it defined assault weapons
solely by naming specific models, without reference to
their fea-tures, 1993 Conn. Pub. Acts No. 93-306, §
1(a)(1), an approach then-Representative Lawlor
defended as providing “the precision that is required
for a criminal statute.” Conn. H.R. Proc., 1993 Reg.
Sess., vol. 36,

The legislation enacted in response to Sandy Hook
would build upon that feature-based framework. Legislative leaders insisted it be both deliberate and bipartisan. The incoming Speaker of the House, Brendan Sharkey, had been meeting with lawmakers from
both parties when news of the shooting broke, and all
of them were deeply shaken. Pinciaro, supra, at 495.
The Speaker resolved that th e response had to be “a
clearly bipartisan measure.” Id. To that end, he bypassed the Judiciary Committee, which Democrats
controlled two to one, and instead sent the bill to a
task force of four Democrats and four Republicans created specifically to produce a bipartisan bill. Id.
CAGV also worked closely, from the outset, with
law enforcement, and police chiefs across the State
supported the  bill. 16  Law enforcement officers
told

legislators what they had seen on the job and what
they feared seeing again: officers responding to an active shooter, outgunned by a civilian carrying a military-style rifle.17 Their testimony resonated with

The resulting law—Public Act 13-3, An Act Concerning Gun Violence Prevention and Children’s
Safety—targets the specific features that make a rifle
unusually dangerous and especially lethal in the
hands of a mass shooter like  the one at Sandy Hook.
2013 Conn. Pub. Acts No. 13-3. Among other things,
the 2013 Act replaced the State’s former two-feature
test for determining whether a semiautomatic rifle is
an “assault weapon” with a one-feature test. Conn.
Gen. Stat. § 53-202a(1)(E)(i). Under that test, a semiautomatic centerfire rifle that can accept a detachable magazine is an assault we apon if it has at least
one of five enumerated features: a folding or telescoping stock; a pistol grip, thumbhole stock, or other grip
that allows a finger other than the trigger finger to sit
below the action; a forwar d pistol grip; a flash suppressor; or a grenade or flare launcher. Id.
The 2013 Act defines a single class of weapons in
two complementary ways. It lists by name a number
of specific rifle models that were in production when
the Act took effect, including the model used at Sandy
Hook, together with copies or duplicates of those models. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53-202a(1)(B). It pairs that
list with a features test that identifies the same class
of rifles by the characteristics they share. Id. § 53-
202a(1)(E)(i). As Senator Donald Williams, then-
President Pro Tempore of the Connecticut Senate, explained in response to questions about the named rifles, “the guns that are on the list meet the criteria of
the physical characteristics test. . . . [T]hose are the
assault weapons, for the most part designed originally
with a military platform, capable of semi-automatic
fire and centerfire as opposed to rimfire.” Conn. S.
Proc., 2013 Reg. Sess., supra, at 658 (statement of

18


Sen. Williams). It is the feat ures test that reaches a
rifle regardless of its name or date of manufacture,
and it was the features test that closed the loophole
manufacturers had exploited under the 1993 law. The
Law is predicated on the notion that the enumerated
features are what make these rifles—like the military
weapons on which they are modeled—accurate, easy
to aim and fire even without training, and capable of
being emptied very quickly.
III. The Law Is Consistent With This Nation’s
Tradition Of Regulating Unusually Dangerous Weapons
Because the Law responded to an unprecedented
societal concern, the question under Bruen’s nuanced
approach is whether the Law is “relevantly similar” to
the laws our tradition permits, judged by “how and
why” it burdens the righ t of armed self-defense. 597
U.S. at 29; Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 692. It is.
Begin with what the Law regulates. Connecticut
did not ban a firearm merely because it looked menacing or unfamiliar. Instead, the legislature identified the specific characteristics that allow a shooter to
fire more rounds, more accurately, and for longer
while making him harder to stop, and it regulated
those characteristics. A f olding or telescoping stock
makes a rifle easier to conceal and to maneuver
through a school hallway. A pistol grip or forward grip
lets a shooter control recoil  and stay on target while
firing rapidly. A flash suppressor hides the shooter’s
position from the people he is shooting at and from the
officers trying to stop him. See Lamont, 153 F.4th at
225–26; see also Rupp, 723 F. Supp. 3d at 854 (finding

19


“undisputed evidence that each of the challenged feature-based restrictions facilitates semiautomatic assault rifles’ danger and disproportionate use in mass
shootings”). And a grenade or flare launcher serves
no legitimate purpose in a civilian home.
Next, consider how the Law burdens the right of
armed self-defense. Apart from the most lethal weapons, firearms without the enumerated features remain lawful, as do the handguns that Heller called
“the quintessential self-defense weapon.” 554 U.S. at
629. The Law “preserv[es] numerous legal alternatives for self-defense and other lawful purposes.” Lamont, 153 F.4th at 222. And residents who lawfully
owned covered rifles before the 2013 Act took effect
were permitted to keep them. See Conn. Gen. Stat. §
53-202d(a)(2). The Law thus leaves law-abiding residents armed and removes only certain unusually dangerous firearms from the market.
As to why the Law imposes that burden, it rests
on the same justification that has animated weapons
regulation in this country from its Founding, and in
English law before that: leg islators identified arms
that were unusually dangerous because of their characteristics and restricted them. See Conn. Resp. Br.
at 10–22. That is the traditi on of regulating “dangerous or unusual weapons” that this Court has recognized, Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 697 (quoting 4 Blackstone,
supra, at 149), and it “encompasses those arms that
legislators determined were unusually dangerous because of their characteristics,” Lamont, 153 F.4th at
233 (emphasis omitted). Heller itself acknowledged
that weapons “most useful in military service—M-16
rifles and the like—may be banned.” 554 U.S. at 627.
The features the Law targets are the very ones that

20


make a civilian rifle most  like its military counterpart.22
That the people of Connecticut have embraced the
legislature’s judgment for more than a decade confirms that the Law’s burden on armed self-defense is
comparably justified. See Bruen, 597 U.S. at 29. In
March 2013, while the bill was still being negotiated,
a Quinnipiac University poll found that Connecticut
voters supported expanding the State’s assault weapons ban by a margin of 68 to 28 percent.23 Support
for the State’s gun laws has remained strong in the
years since. The General A ssembly strengthened the
2013 Act in 2023. See 2023 Conn. Pub. Acts No. 23-53.
And although the people of Connecticut have had
more than a decade and several election cycles in
which to undo what their legislators did in 2013, they
have cho-sen to keep it.
For CAGV, the 2013 Act was the culmination of
twenty years of work; it closed the gaps that the organization had been trying to close since its founding.
And it has seen results. In the years since, Connecticut has consistently ranked among the States with the
